body: Why are you using a resolved promise here? Is it to be sure that the code executed after everything else?
Yes and you need the try/catch to catch the error if the expect fails.

Why do we base our implementation on promises? Why not just use setTimeout(..., 0)?

```js
defer = f => { setTimeout(f,0); }
```

After some searching it seems the current fastest way to express "Please execute this code asynchronously as soon as possible" is to actually use Promise.resolve().then().

https://jakearchibald.com/2015/tasks-microtasks-queues-and-schedules and https://jakearchibald.com/2015/tasks-microtasks-queues-and-schedules/#comment-2926206647

I also asked @developit for his advice on this, we can wait a bit before merging.

Did you try to write a simple test case without any of our code just to try return Promise.resolve().then(throw..)? maybe there's a bug somewhere or a misunderstanding of ours on how promise works with jest

It uses the preact implementation for doing stuff async as soon as possible. The guy even publish a benchmark of the different options.
See: https://github.com/developit/preact/commit/6954d7549f35b5c32421c6855ee29ffda01137d1 and https://esbench.com/bench/55d4d44e2efbca1100bf7251

We can agree on supporting only browsers with Promise.resolve(), http://caniuse.com/#feat=promises

And delegate promise polyfill to the user.
Do you need fake timers in the end>?
Note: on the benchmark you might get better results with other implementations but Promise.resolve() is widely supported while others are not
We will explain how to include a polyfill if that's necessary.
